Does “rtk” reduce Claude Code token usage?

Part 2 of a series where we take public “token saving” add-ons for coding agents and run the same paired A/B benchmark against each of them. Part 1 was the caveman skill (advertised −65%, measured −8.5%).

TL;DR: rtk advertised saving: 60–90%. Measured on real agent work: +7.6% more expensive at low reasoning effort (p=0.004), ±0% at high effort. Setup: Claude Code 2.1.201 · claude-sonnet-5 low and high efforts · SkillsBench. Task quality: unchanged in both arms, at both effort levels.

What rtk promises
−60–90%
token cut per its README; −80% in its own demo session
Best it could do here
≈−3%
most of what the model reads never passes through rtk — computed for free before spending a cent
What we actually paid
+7.6%
MORE per typical task with rtk installed (80 tasks, low effort, p=0.004). With high effort: no difference at all
Task quality
no change
across 151 paired tasks: 10 slightly better, 8 slightly worse, 133 identical — a coin flip
Why we ran this

rtk (“Rust Token Killer”) is a CLI proxy with a simple, appealing pitch: your agent runs git status, rtk intercepts it, runs the real command, and hands the model a compressed version of the output — * master / M a.txt / ?? b.txt instead of eleven lines of porcelain. A Claude Code PreToolUse hook rewrites eligible shell commands transparently, so the model doesn’t even have to know rtk exists. The README promises 60–90% less token consumption and walks through a 30-minute session where 118k tokens of command output become 24k.

The compression itself is real and often tasteful. Here is rtk on a live repo, captured from our test container:

# git status                              # rtk git status
On branch master                          * master
Changes not staged for commit:             M a.txt
  (use "git add <file>..." to update…)   ?? b.txt
    modified:   a.txt
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include…)
    b.txt
no changes added to commit …

# python -m pytest  (19 lines)            # rtk pytest
…full pytest output…                      Pytest: 2 passed, 1 failed
                                          Failures:
                                          1. [FAIL] test_fail
                                               test_demo.py:3: in test_fail
                                               E  AssertionError: one is not two

We liked the idea enough to test it properly. Two questions the README doesn’t answer:

First, how much of a real agent session is Bash output at all? The savings table assumes the agent shells out for everything. But Claude Code reads files with its built-in Read tool, searches with Grep, and both bypass the Bash hook completely (rtk’s docs acknowledge this). Whatever those tools carry, rtk can never touch.

Second, does compression cost correctness? A filter that summarizes test output is making an editorial judgment about what the model needs. If it drops the one line that mattered, the agent re-runs commands, reads files raw, or, worse, declares victory on a failing build. Token savings that come with a quality tax are not savings.

Setup

### Result
"o usage errors and retries), a few compression-induced re-reads, and a lot of ordinary variance on the extreme pairs. A thin, systematic tax rather than a dramatic failure.

One real task, watched step by step

How much the model had to re-read at every step of the same task, with and without rtk. The rtk session took MORE steps and ended with a BIGGER pile.

Each rtk-compressed result is indeed smaller — but this session took seven extra steps, and every extra step re-reads the whole history again. That re-reading is most of an agent's bill.
data as table
Finding 3: At high effort, even the penalty disappears

“You only tested at low reasoning effort” was the obvious critique, so we ran all 86 tasks again at high effort – the most expensive single run of the series. Result: the cost penalty does not replicate there. Median paired delta +0.1% (p=0.99), turns +0.0 (p=0.74), quality still tied. At high effort, the model seems to waste fewer turns reacting to compressed output; though at k=1 all we can say is that the penalty didn’t show up there, not that the two effort regimes probably differ. Either way, at no point did rtk save anything.

Does it change when the model thinks harder? Low vs high effort

Solid square = low effort · hollow square = high effort. A marker on the zero line means rtk made no difference.

+14%
At high effort the extra steps and re-reading vanish, and the cost penalty goes with them. But look at fresh tokens — the thing rtk compresses: flat at both settings. The promised savings never appear anywhere.
data as table
Finding 4: Quality survives

The scary failure modes from rtk’s issue tracker including over-filtered test output, masked exit codes, pipes fed compressed text, they barely materialized. A forensic pass over the six smoke pairs with the biggest turn deltas found exactly one broken rewrite (the same compound-find failure mode the full run hit) and one case of the agent deliberately bypassing the hook, across ~150 Bash calls. In those transcripts no recovery files were read and no compressed pipe produced a wrong count (the full runs saw exactly one recovery-file read); the extra turns were overwhelmingly the model choosing different solution paths, not rtk confusion. On the full runs, task scores landed at 5 better / 4 worse / 71 tie at low effort and 5 / 4 / 62 at high (sign test p=1.0 both); showing the arms are statistically indistinguishable on quality, with partial credit counted.

One honest asterisk: on one task (dialogue-parser) rtk’s own binary refused to start inside the task’s image (it needs a newer glibc), so the with-rtk trial died at setup in both full runs while the plain arm scored 0.667. Paired analysis excludes that task from both arms, but it’s a real compatibility failure, not Docker noise. Even scoring every errored trial as zero, the arms stay tied (sign test p=1.0).

Did rtk break anything? The same 80 tasks, scored with and without it

Low-effort run shown; the high-effort run looks the same (5 better, 4 worse, 62 tied).

better with rtk (5)
identical score (71)
worse with rtk (4)
6%
89%
5%
A statistical coin flip — no damage, no improvement. (Honest caveat: ~80 tasks can only rule out big effects; catching a subtle few-point shift would take ~700 runs per side.)
data as table
Finding 5: rtk’s own scoreboard vs the bill

This is the finding that explains the gap. Across the low-effort full run, rtk’s built-in analytics (rtk gain) reported 96.2 million tokens saved — 99.8% of everything it touched; while the measured bill for the same trials went up. Three mechanisms make the scoreboard read high:

First, rtk counts the full raw output as its counterfactual. One cat of a 1.2 MB CSV logged 320k tokens “saved”, but Claude Code truncates any tool result long before 320k tokens; so the agent would have received a few thousand either way. The full run logged 190 of such giant reads at an average of ~506k “saved” tokens each. Second, rtk estimates tokens as chars÷4 at the moment of execution, while most of a session’s input cost is cached re-reads billed at a tenth of the price. Third, the hook simply never sees the majority of context. The scoreboard is grading its own homework.

What rtk promises per command — and what its own logs recorded

Hollow square = the README's promised cut · solid square = what actually happened across all 86 tasks, per rtk's own logs. (git's promises span −75…−92 by subcommand; hollow shows git status, −80.)

actually delivered
promised (hollow)
git (status/log/add…) (only 4 uses)
test runners (pytest/cargo/mvn…)
grep / rg (search)
ls / tree / find / wc (listings)
cat / read (file dumps) † (not a real saving)
0%
−25%
−50%
−75%
−100%
† the grey marker is bookkeeping, not savings: rtk credits itself with the FULL size of giant files it 'compressed', but Claude Code would have cut those down anyway — nobody was ever going to be billed for them. It's the only row that beats its promise. Every honest row falls short.
data as table
Verdict

Honest engineering, wrong counterfactual. We wanted this one to win; the demo is genuinely satisfying to play with. The filters are real and often elegant; quality doesn’t suffer; the hook mechanism works exactly as designed. But on real agentic coding work the advertised 60–90% never had anywhere to live: the hook only ever sees about a fifth of the tool output, Claude Code already truncates the pathological outputs rtk brags about compressing, and the cached re-reads that dominate input cost bill at a tenth of the price. What’s left is a measured median +7.6% cost increase at low effort and a flat zero at high effort, a thin tax from a broken rewrite here and an extra exploration turn there, never a saving.

The deeper lesson generalizes beyond rtk: a tool’s self-reported savings are a claim about its counterfactual, not about your bill. rtk’s scoreboard said 96 million tokens saved while the invoice went up. If you evaluate any context-compression tool, measure the paired bill, not the tool’s diff.

Methodology notes

Same discipline as part 1, learned the expensive way:

Never trust k=1. The run ladder was: free transcript replay → 1-trial wiring check → 10 Bash-heavy tasks at k=1 → the same 10 at k=3 → the full 86 at k=1, twice (low and high effort). Per-task scores flip freely between attempts in both arms; only paired deltas that survive the ladder get reported.
Paired analysis only. Every number compares the same task across arms under the same job; tasks that errored in either arm are excluded from both. Quality uses an exact sign test over non-ties; token/cost deltas use per-task medians plus Wilcoxon signed-rank, because arm totals are outlier-dominated, a single session crossing the 200k long-context pricing tier can bill 25× normal and flip a raw total.
Endpoints"

Anastasia Kazakova
October 15, 2026

Netflix plugged JetBrains’ headless code-intelligence engine – the same one behind IntelliJ IDEA – into Claude Code and Codex, then benchmarked it against a variety of scenarios. The details and numbers are available below.

At a glance
Company	Netflix – Application Development Platform (ADP), GenAI Platform, and Agentic SDLC teams
Challenge	Coding agents were struggling to navigate Java/Kotlin code, especially across compiled library (JAR) boundaries
Technology	JetBrains IDE code intelligence for Java, built on the same code-indexing engine that powers IntelliJ IDEA, run headlessly with no IDE open.
Netflix’s role	Built the daemon and CLI needed to make the LSP callable by an agent – infrastructure that JetBrains hadn’t shipped yet
Result	Typically 20–30% more efficient (fewer tokens, less time), and up to about 65% in the best case, on real programming tasks – the size of the gain depends on the model, the agent, and the task, generally larger for stronger models and higher effort settings
Evaluated on	Two real codebases – an internal production service and Netflix’s open-source DGS Framework – across several current coding agents and models, July–August 2026
The goal: Increase agent ROI

JetBrains and Netflix set out to give coding agents accurate, IntelliJ IDEA-grade code understanding in headless environments – with no IntelliJ IDEA instance running.

“Coding agents like Claude Code are slow and unreliable at navigating Java/Kotlin code, especially across library (JAR) boundaries. We integrated a headless JetBrains IDE’s code engine to give agents IntelliJ IDE-grade code intelligence in headless environments, with no IDE running. We created a benchmark with real programming tasks, which shows that with the JetBrains IDE’s code engine, agents are consistently more efficient – using fewer tokens and less time, with the exact gain depending on the model.”

— Paul Bakker, Staff Software Engineer, Netflix

The JAR problem Netflix is trying to solve that Paul describes above: JVM projects typically ship libraries as JAR files only, never as source. Agents have to unzip the JARs (guessing which ones matter), potentially decompile class files, then grep through that incomplete view.

The solution: JetBrains IDE intelligence

JetBrains has spent years building the code intelligence engine behind IntelliJ IDEA. It is based on a deterministic index of your project source files, including all libraries. This intelligence is now exposed via an LSP and available in VS Code-compatible editors. Netflix worked with a headless build of that engine.

The LSP alone isn’t enough for a coding agent to use directly: It’s just a server speaking a protocol, with no easy way for an agent to call it and no built-in process management to reuse a running instance between calls. Netflix closed that gap themselves using the daemon and CLI described in the next section.

Architecture in detail: Keeping the index warm

Building an index for a project takes real time, just as opening a large project in IntelliJ IDEA for the first time does. A coding agent calls the LSP in many small, fine-grained steps, and a realistic task needs several such calls. If each one spun up a fresh LSP server, every single call would incur a multi-second cold-start cost – even on a project whose index had already been built a minute earlier.

A daemon process is required to avoid the overhead of cold-starting the LSP server process on repeated calls. JetBrains is working on delivering a daemon, but no daemon was available by the time of evaluation, so Netflix has built one for their own needs:

Each tool call was short-lived and stateless – it just shelled out to the CLI.
The daemon is the part that stays up: Its session manager routes each call by project root to the matching server process, which holds that project’s index in memory.
A second call against the same project skips indexing entirely and goes straight to a warm server over stdio.
Both the daemon and CLI are developed in Java and distributed as a GraalVM executable, so there is no startup or runtime overhead from the JVM.
How Netflix measured the ROI of JetBrains IDE intelligence

To understand if (and to what extent) JetBrains IDE intelligence improves the performance of a coding agent, a benchmark suite was developed. Same model, same task, same codebase – the only variable was whether the agent could invoke the JetBrains IDE intelligence. Results are reported as the performance difference between runs with JetBrains IDE intelligence versus runs without it.

Evaluation environment and approach:

Datasets	Two real codebases: An internal service (medium-size project) using Spring Boot 4 and Gradle.
Netflix’s own open-source DGS Framework – a public, mixed Kotlin/Java GraphQL framework.
Tasks	Two task types:
Small/focused tasks where the agent attempts to understand specifics in the codebase, e.g. “where is this interface used in the project”, “what implementations exist of this interface”, “what is the structure of this class”.
Full end-to-end tasks, such as implementing a new feature, refactoring a class, or removing code.
Models	Claude Code with Opus 5 (medium/high effort)
Claude Code with Sonnet 5 (medium/high effort)
Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol (medium/high effort)
Scoring	While the most important metrics in the experiment were token consumption and time to completion, LLM as a judge was implemented for checking correctness. It works against a reference change set for end-to-end tasks and applies deterministic scoring metric for navigation tasks.
Outlier handling	A task that crashed, hit a budget cap, or thrashed in either arm was excluded from both, so one blow-up couldn’t skew the comparison.

The benchmarks were run multiple times to validate the results and see the effects of changes from new LSP releases.

Across every model, agent, and task type tested, JetBrains IDE intelligence made coding agents more efficient overall – typically 20–30% more efficient, and up to about 65% in the best case, depending on the specific model, agent, and task. The stronger models, with higher effort, saw the largest gains. These models are more expensive, so efficiency improvements matter more, but these models are also better at using indexes effectively.

Efficiency gain per configuration, combining token and time savings. Each comparison runs the same task, model, and codebase twice – once with JetBrains IDE intelligence available, once without it.

~25%
AVERAGE GAIN
20–30%
TYPICAL RANGE
~65%
BEST CASE
CONFIGURATION	CODE NAVIGATION	END-TO-END
Strongest model, high effort	~65%	~24%
Mid model, high effort	~29%	~30%
Mid model, medium effort	~24%	~22%
Lighter configuration, high effort	~17%*	~21%

Figures are a snapshot and will shift with new model releases.

These numbers are a snapshot, not a fixed benchmark result. Every new model release changes how agents search, reason, and use tools, so the exact percentages will keep moving – which is why this write-up reports ranges rather than per-model results. What held up across Netflix’s runs is the general shape: every model and agent tested became more efficient, the largest gains came from the strongest model at a high-effort setting, and the size of the gain differed noticeably from one model to the next.

Code-navigation tasks: More efficient across the board, correctness held or improved

Every model and effort level tested used fewer tokens with JetBrains IDE intelligence – no exceptions there – with savings ranging from roughly 15% to 60%. The size of the gain depended mostly on the model: the strongest model saw by far the largest improvements, while lighter-weight configurations landed at the lower end of both ranges. Correctness held steady in most runs and improved in two – it never dropped.

For the code-navigation tasks specifically, one tool/model combination already batches multiple search calls into a single command, so both with and without JetBrains IDE intelligence, it only makes one tool call there. Calling into JetBrains IDE intelligence is a little slower for that one call than the batched search command – which is what produced the clear lack of time benefit for that combination, not a fair reflection of real-world use. That’s why the broader end-to-end task suite is the more reliable read on time instead, where JetBrains IDE intelligence was faster across every model and agent tested.

On the expanded end-to-end run, correctness held steady everywhere across every model and agent tested, so the benefit shows up entirely in efficiency, not in whether the task got done. Every model and agent combination was roughly 10–30% more efficient with JetBrains IDE intelligence, looking at time to completion and token spend. A lot of this is explained by requiring fewer tool calls to come to the same conclusions.

Before committing to the described approach, Netflix ruled out two others. The first rejected was a homegrown internal CLI that connected to a running IntelliJ IDEA instance to get access to a project index. The process is similar to what this article describes, but it requires an IDE to be running. This approach didn’t fit headless agents for environments like Otto, Bitbot, distributed refactoring tooling, CI, etc.

Second, an existing Eclipse LSP, which is used for Java in VS Code, was considered. But for Netflix’s build system (Gradle-based), it just didn’t work.

What’s next
Where Netflix goes from here

After the test, Netflix concluded that “the benchmarks show that there is a benefit to having a deterministic intelligence layer alongside your agent”. Of course, it doesn’t cut every coding-agent task by a fixed percentage. But for this specific problem – resolving real structure across JAR boundaries – the benefit is large, holds across models, and doesn’t cost anything in correctness.

Netflix plans to run the same benchmark methodology against Python, TypeScript/JavaScript, and Go. Coding agents for those languages have similar problems. But of course, the ways libraries are downloaded in a project vary by language, so the mechanics of the issues and possible solutions differ. JetBrains plans to continue the collaboration and support this evaluation further.

JetBrains’ take: The LSP is just one step, not the destination

JetBrains IDE intelligence for Java has been tested by Netflix and is now shipped as part of the Java & Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA extension. JetBrains also continues experiments with the LSP+CLI approach and will report the results once ready.

The LSP’s basic primitive is a position in a text document. The specification defines a position as “between two characters, like an insert cursor in an editor”. That’s a natural primitive for a human working at a keyboard. But agents don’t really think in terms of cursor locations. They ask questions about the program, like “Why is this call inside createUser() unresolved?” and “Which tests are covering this method?”, etc. It’s about understanding relationships between parts of the code rather than looking at cursor positions. And a text position is a fragile identity – inserting one character before any given position causes that position to move.

What an agent needs isn’t a sharper cursor, but a layer that provides answers formulated in the same way as the tasks themselves – i.e. in terms of symbols, diagnostics, test relations, runtime behavior – and returns enough context to reason about the answer, not just locations in a text document.

“That’s what I mean by a code engine: not another protocol that lets an agent imitate editor interaction, but a set of precise operations over program structure and execution – one that returns enough context to actually reason about the result. LSP is useful, but it shouldn’t define the final agent-facing abstraction. Build agent tooling as if the agent were a tiny human at an editor, and you force it to speak in cursor coordinates. Agents need a code engine, not a virtual editor.”

— Aleksey Stukalov, IDE Division Lead, JetBrains

The Netflix numbers prove code intelligence is worth paying for. Deciding what shape that intelligence takes is the challenge that lies ahead.

content.text:
I read both JetBrains posts in full through Playwright. The first one, on rtk, applies directly to your setup, since your global CLAUDE.md uses it. The Netflix post turned out to be about code intelligence, not design.

## rtk (Rust Token Killer)

JetBrains ran the same paired benchmark as for Caveman. The setup was Claude Code 2.1.201 with `claude-sonnet-5` at low and high effort, SkillsBench with 86 tasks, and rtk v0.43.0 installed exactly as `rtk init -g` ships it (binary, PreToolUse hook and RTK.md). That is the same install your CLAUDE.md describes. Total spend was about $320 over 425 billed trials.

| | Claimed | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Token cut | −60% to −90% | Fresh input tokens changed by +3.2% (low effort) and +4.3% (high effort), both within noise |
| Cost at low effort | Lower | **+7.6% more expensive** per task (80 tasks, p = 0.004), with 13.8% more turns and 14.3% more cache reads |
| Cost at high effort | Lower | No difference (+0.1%, p = 0.99) |
| Task quality | Unchanged | Unchanged: 5 better, 4 worse, 71 tied at low effort (p = 1.0) |

JetBrains's explanation:

- **A structural ceiling of about 3%.** Of 1,056 shell commands replayed from 83 baseline transcripts, only a third were something rtk can rewrite. Half were `python3`, project scripts or loops with no rule, and the rest use shell syntax rtk skips on purpose. Claude Code's built-in Read and Grep tools bypass the Bash hook entirely, and rtk's README admits this. So only about a fifth of tool output was compressible, and even squeezing all of it by 70% caps out near 3%.
- **The cost increase** appears to come from sessions running longer. More steps mean the model re-reads its history more times, and most of the bill is cached re-reads. Heavily rewritten task pairs cost about 24% more, versus 5% for pairs the hook barely touched. JetBrains found no single villain, just a few broken rewrites (compound `find` predicates), some compression-induced re-reads and ordinary variance.
- **`rtk gain` is not your bill.** Its own analytics reported 96.2 million tokens saved while the measured bill went up. It counts the full raw output as the counterfactual (one `cat` of a 1.2 MB file logged 320k "saved" tokens, though Claude Code would have truncated it anyway). It also estimates tokens as characters ÷ 4, while most input cost is cached re-reads billed at a tenth of the price.
- **One real compatibility failure.** The rtk binary refused to start in one task's image because it needs a newer glibc.

JetBrains's verdict: "Honest engineering, wrong counterfactual." The filters are real and the quality is fine. The advertised savings had nowhere to live in agentic coding. Their general lesson: "a tool's self-reported savings are a claim about its counterfactual, not about your bill."

**Limits of applying it to you:**
- The benchmark is SkillsBench tasks on Sonnet 5, not your Playwright-heavy front-end sessions. Browser output isn't touched by rtk either way.
- The full runs were k=1, and 80 tasks can only rule out large effects. JetBrains says catching a subtle few-point quality shift would need about 700 runs per side.
- Your own sessions might differ. I haven't touched your rtk config, and I wouldn't change it on this evidence alone. If you want to know, the clean test is to compare paired real tasks with the hook on and off, using actual billed cost and not `rtk gain`.

## Netflix + JetBrains code intelligence (Oct 15, 2026)

- **What it is.** Netflix's Application Development Platform, GenAI Platform and Agentic SDLC teams plugged JetBrains's headless code-intelligence engine into Claude Code and Codex. It targets Java and Kotlin navigation, especially across compiled JAR boundaries, where agents otherwise unzip, decompile and grep. Netflix built the daemon (to keep the index warm) and CLI (to make the language server callable by an agent) because JetBrains hadn't shipped them.
- **Results.** Typically 20–30% more efficient (average of token and time savings), up to about 65% in the best case, with correctness held or improved in every run. Gains were largest for the strongest model at high effort.
  - Tested on Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol.
  - Two codebases: an internal Spring Boot service and Netflix's open-source DGS Framework.
  - Two task types: navigation questions and end-to-end tasks.
  - A crashed or thrashing task was excluded from both arms.
  - Correctness was judged against a reference change set (LLM-as-judge for end-to-end tasks, deterministic scoring for navigation).
- **Caveats.** It's a JetBrains-hosted case study, so treat it as vendor-curated. The 65% best case is navigation with the strongest model, and the end-to-end gains were roughly 21–30%. One configuration's time comparison was unrepresentative because it batches search calls into a single command. The numbers are a snapshot that will shift with new models. Netflix plans to repeat this for Python, TypeScript and JavaScript, and Go.
- **It says nothing about design or front-end workflows.** It doesn't answer our earlier Netflix question.

## What this adds to our picture

1. **Deterministic layers beat prompt tricks.** Netflix's conclusion is that there is a benefit "to having a deterministic intelligence layer alongside your agent." That is the same principle as uSpec's extraction, Atlassian's CLI, Spectrum's audit rubric and Salesforce's linter-as-gate. JetBrains's point that agents need answers in terms of symbols, diagnostics and test relations, not cursor positions, has a front-end equivalent. That would be a query layer over computed styles, the accessibility tree, tokens and component usage, not a model reading CSS.
2. **A relevant precedent in this repo.** A recent commit (`f10e6b8`) added language-service evidence guidance to smith. Netflix's results are independent support for that direction, and the same idea could extend to UI evidence.
3. **Token savers need a paired bill measurement.** Both JetBrains posts used the same method: a free transcript replay first, then a small run, a repeated run, and the full run, with paired per-task medians and Wilcoxon tests and with failed tasks excluded from both arms. That is the template for any `mason:evaluate` work, including the muse gate and the sketch-mode proposal. Their "never trust k=1" warning applies to our 51-call gate count too, since it comes from one project.
4. **Effort level interacts with everything.** Both rtk's penalty and Netflix's gains depended on effort. Our tier choices should be evaluated at the effort we'll actually run.

I think the research side is now broad enough. The remaining gaps are the internal cost data from our own transcripts and the unverified items flagged earlier. Do you want to move to drafting the proposal now?

Its `rtk gain` scoreboard doesn't reflect the bill. Netflix's post is a vendor case study on Java code intelligence (20–30% typical efficiency gain), not design. Both support deterministic tool layers and paired-bill evals. No repo files were modified.

# Decision Records

Decide whether an architectural choice needs a durable record, and write the record so a later reader with no memory of the discussion does not silently reverse it. A record preserves the reason behind a decision, so nobody accepts it blindly or reverses it blindly.

## Write one only when both gates pass

- **Architectural:** the choice sets a boundary, a model, a direction, or a rule that several changes must respect.
- **Expensive to reverse or not obvious from the code:** a reader who sees only the code would plausibly undo it, or undoing it would be costly.

One decision per record. A choice that fails a gate belongs elsewhere.

| Fact | Home |
| :--- | :--- |
| Architecture, model, direction, decision, rejected alternative | Decision record in `docs/adr/` |
| Rule for every session: command, invariant, style, routing | `AGENTS.md` |
| Required behavior | Spec |
| How the system works today | Docs |
| Why one change was made | Commit message |
| Personal preference or correction for one repository | Agent memory, uncommitted |

Agent memory is unshared and goes stale, so a decision never lives only there.

## Form

Title, status, context, decision, options considered, consequences. Each rejected option carries its "because". Keep a record to one or two pages. Records written before this form may state the alternatives inside the context; leave them as written.

Add an `Enforced by` line only when a test, lint, type, or hook enforces the decision. A decision that a check can enforce should have the check; the record explains why it exists.

Add one line to the `docs/adr/README.md` index in the form `Do not <X> without a new ADR`, for a decision an agent could undo without noticing.

## Prose

Keep the causal "because" and the rejected alternative. Cut narration of the discussion, restated code, and hedging. Write one paragraph per line; do not hard-wrap.

## Status and change

Do not rewrite an accepted record's context, decision, or options; the reasoning at the time is what the record preserves. Update its status and links, and fix errors that do not change its meaning. To change a decision, write a new record that supersedes it and mark the old one superseded; the old record stays. Keep the active set small by writing records only for decisions that pass both gates.

## Refutation and disposition

content.text:
The evidence points to a small set of changes in a clear order. The first changes only cost wording and bookkeeping. The larger additions (a sketch mode, a render-evidence capability) come after that. Your instinct also holds up in the evidence: the gated pipeline earned its keep on stable contracts, and exploration was where it hurt.

## What the evidence says, in four points

1. **The pipeline works for behavior and fails for appearance.** The gates caught real contradictions, accessibility values and cross-spec conflicts. Every visible defect was found by a human look, an audit, or the 16 Oct suite. The cause is structural: `spec@1` has no way to express visual intent, and nothing renders anything.
2. **Gate churn is mostly wording.** The 51 `muse:exit-gate` calls were fix-and-resubmit loops. Anthropic's own docs warn that a reviewer told to find gaps "will usually report some, even when the work is sound." Gates also ignored their own retry cap.
3. **Exploration needs a different mode, not a looser pipeline.** You asked for it explicitly, both vendors' guidance supports it, and Vercel's mode routing is the best example. It is an aviation-style IFR/VFR split with an explicit promote step.
4. **Deterministic layers beat prompt tricks.** uSpec (extraction), Atlassian (CLI/MCP), Salesforce (linter-as-gate), Netflix (code intelligence) and the JetBrains tests all point the same way. Token-saving prompts (caveman, rtk) did little.

## Where each change goes

| Plugin or layer | Change | Driven by |
|---|---|---|
| **muse** | Fix the dangling "ranger accessibility taxonomy" reference (in `plugin.json`, README and SKILL.md). Move its `verdict@1` to `verdict@3`. Add a `spec@2` with fields for token and visual references (a story id, a screenshot path). Load ARIA pattern reference tables before drafting. Add a ground-truth step that extracts tokens and geometry so the drafter stops inventing numbers. | A, D, uSpec |
| **muse (new skills)** | `sketch`: mode-routed, option files with stable IDs and statuses (open, parked, chosen, rejected) that double as the decision log, TBDs allowed, no gate. `promote`: derive a spec from the chosen prototype. | B, C, Vercel, Magic Patterns, Pocock's `prototype` skill |
| **smith** | A `spike` skill that skips plan, spec, mutator and exit-gate and reports what was and wasn't verified. A UI verification recipe that requires rendered evidence. | A, B, Fluent |
| **navigator** | File ownership per task, single writer for token and shared files, a shared-contract step before sibling specs, and supersession handling. | C, parallel-agent research |
| **sentinel / ranger** | Add render, lint and copy-provenance checks as evidence kinds. Build the missing accessibility hazard pack, or remove the references to it. | D, Primer, SLDS, avoid-ai-design |
| **scribe** | Extend `spec-drift` to cover design-intent files and tie reviews to the source versions they covered. | uSpec, TanStack Intent |
| **mason** | A link-checker for cross-plugin references (it would have caught the dangling one), and the paired-eval harness. | A, JetBrains |
| **shared/constitution** | Gate hygiene: a "no findings" pass is valid, blockers must cite evidence, wording-only fixes happen outside the gate, and any override is logged. A small fixed vocabulary for verdicts and handoffs. | C, Anthropic, ICAO |

## Constraints from the ADRs

I read the decision records, and several of these changes need new ADRs, not just edits:

- **ADR 003 (cognitive-mode separation).** A sketch agent that generates and compares options is a divergent mode the tier model doesn't have, and combining generation with judgment needs a new ADR.
- **ADR 004 (immutable schemas).** Nothing is edited in place. `spec@2`, `verdict`, `workspace-manifest@2` (for browser and visual capabilities) and any `reasoning` rename each require a new version. Renaming `reasoning` touches 29 of 31 schemas, which is a large change on the strength of one unverified claim.
- **ADR 005 (artifact-agnostic gate).** The gate can't become UI-specific. Visual evidence has to arrive as a generic evidence kind through recon capabilities, not as a UI branch in sentinel.
- **ADR 001 and 006 (fixed sections, byte-identical constitution).** The Anthropic report suggests these may be unnecessary overhead on newer models, but that is inference. Test it with an ablation before proposing anything.
- **ADR 008 (drop test-first ordering)** is the precedent for relaxing rigidity, and a good template for the spike-mode ADR.

Every change also needs its Codex counterpart and `just marketplace-sync`, per `shared/harness-authoring.md`.

## Suggested order

**Tier 0 — measure first and fix the defects (small, low risk)**
- Fix the dangling muse reference and migrate muse to `verdict@3`.
- Record baselines from the transcripts: gate rounds per spec, blockers split into wording vs substantive, time to the first visual, and defects found after gates.
- Run a small paired test of the `reasoning` field concern on one agent before touching 29 schemas.

**Tier 1 — gate hygiene (mostly prompt and constitution text)**
- Evidence-citing blockers, "no findings" as a valid pass, and a logged override in place of the silent one.
- Orchestrator-enforced retry cap.
- Readback in the drafter and gate correction loop, and the small fixed vocabulary.

**Tier 2 — the two new modes**
- Sketch plus promote in muse, and spike in smith.
- A render-evidence capability, with screenshots per viewport, theme and state plus axe and console output.
- `spec@2` with visual references.

**Tier 3 — the supporting layer**
- A routed design-intent file for art direction (not a monolithic DESIGN.md, given Atlassian's token-cost result).
- Lint-style checks for tokens, copy and slop patterns.
- Ground-truth extraction, file ownership in plans and drift coverage for intent files.

## What to avoid

- **Micro-optimizations like caveman and rtk.** The evidence shows small or no gains.
- **A big monolithic design file.** Atlassian measured it at about twice the tokens of the MCP and found it lost information.
- **A hard dependency on Figma.** Your workflow was code-first, so make the design source an optional input.
- **Loosening gates for stable contracts.** The SiteNav work (478 passing e2e tests) shows the strict path pays off once ideas are narrowed.
- **Trusting small evals.** Use paired runs and the bill, per the JetBrains method.

## Gaps that could change this

- All transcript evidence comes from two sessions in one project.
- Several research claims are second-hand or unverified. They include the `reasoning_extraction` refusal behavior, Figma Make's depth, and the OpenAI model pages that returned 403.
- I haven't measured what the gates cost in tokens or time.

## Next step

I'd write the Tier 0 baseline script and a design proposal that bundles Tier 1 and the sketch/promote skills, with draft ADRs for the two that need them (the divergent mode and `spec@2`). Do you want that proposal, or would you rather start with the Tier 0 fixes?

Several items need new ADRs, notably 003, 004 and 005. No repo files were modified.

message.content: Does this account for my guidance on exploratory and front-end ideation along with all the learnings from anthropic, openai, others in the industry, agents.md, uber uspec, etc, etc?

content.text:
Partly. The plan covers the main findings, but it drops several things I found earlier, and one choice cuts against your priority. I checked it against what we gathered.

## Covered

| Input | Where it shows up in the plan |
|---|---|
| Your guidance on loose exploration | Sketch, promote and spike modes, with no gates |
| "See designs" | Option files and a rendered matrix across brands and themes |
| Anthropic | Gate hygiene, evidence-citing blockers, "no findings" as a valid pass, and ablation before removing structure |
| Uber uSpec | Ground-truth extraction, ARIA reference tables and a human-readable spec rendering |
| Vercel, Atlassian, Spectrum, Salesforce, Primer | Mode routing, a routed intent file instead of a monolith, and lint-style gates |
| JetBrains and Netflix | Paired, bill-based evals |
| ICAO | Fixed vocabulary, readback and logged overrides |

## Thin

- **"Validate that tools work."** You said this alongside "see designs." I folded it into a smith spike mode, but never designed it. A spike that checks a library or tool actually works in your stack is a distinct job from visual sketching.
- **Sketch rendering medium.** In your sessions you moved off Claude Artifacts to local pages and Playwright screenshots. The plan doesn't say where sketches render, or how they land in a repo.
- **Decision persistence.** You hit "did you lose that decision" repeatedly, and docs went stale within a day. I mentioned a decision log in the sketch skill, but not how decisions reach future sessions or how that fits the repo's own table (ADRs for decisions, AGENTS.md for session rules). I never read the `pages` AGENTS.md, which is the actual AGENTS.md instance in your own work.
- **Codex.** I noted that counterparts are needed. I left out the specific changes M2 found: outcome-first wording, no effort `none`, a short AGENTS.md pointer because of the 32 KiB cap, and TOML subagents.

## Dropped from the plan

These were in the research notes but did not reach the plan table:
- **Anti-slop and taste controls.** Anthropic's guidance to propose about four distinct visual directions and have the user pick one, ban lists, rejection clauses, and the deterministic scanner idea. This is most of the front-end ideation guidance.
- **Vercel's `coverage-gaps.md`** and its rule that a rule candidate stays pending until a human accepts it.
- **Stalls.** Oversized spec and plan files hung agents (17 failed tasks, 32 "stalled" mentions). ICAO's lost-contact procedures and Anthropic's context guidance both bear on this, and the plan has no fix.
- **Orchestrator owns subagent spawning.** Anthropic flagged agents spawning their own verifiers as harmful.
- **Evals for the new skills.** shadcn and Vercel test their skill rules with evals. The plan covers eval infrastructure but not evaluating the sketch skill itself.
- **Copy and voice work.** Case studies and landing copy had no plugin coverage, and I only added a provenance check.
- **Effort-level evaluation.** Gate tiers should be tested at the effort we'd actually run.
- **Brad Frost's three layers** (rules, MCP, AGENTS.md) as the way to organize design intent.

## An ordering problem

I ordered the tiers by risk and coupling, which puts sketch mode in Tier 2 behind gate hygiene. Your stated priority was exploration. Sketch mode is a pure addition with the least coupling to existing agents. It needs a new ADR, but it would be the first thing you could use. I think it should go first, after the small Tier 0 fixes.

## Limits of the research

- uSpec: I read the docs and blog but not its repo, so I don't know how its skill files structure the reference tables.
- Several claims are second-hand or unverified, including the `reasoning` refusal behavior, so my confidence in that rename is low.
- The plan came from one synthesis pass and hasn't been checked line by line against the notes.

## Proposed fix

I can build a traceability matrix before we draft anything: every finding in the notes (A–D, R1–R4, S1–S3, M1–M2 plus the JetBrains and ICAO items) mapped to a plan item, or explicitly deferred or rejected with a reason. That would expose gaps like the ones above systematically. It would also reorder the plan with sketch first and add a concrete design for the spike and decision-persistence pieces.

Do you want that matrix, with the plan revised from it?

# Wisp Plugins validation and formatting.

Confidence tags: [P] primary page read in full or via Playwright; [S] search summary; [K] author's own knowledge, not fetched; [U] unverified.

## U. User guidance (verbatim intent, from this session)
- U1: "the plugin workflows are too rigid for early/experimental and idea work where we might be more flexible to vibe-coded iffiness but we want to flush ideas out, see designs, validate that tools work without worrying about tests, specs, etc."
- U2: Wants to understand the work done on two brands/sites (techworx, orin-dx), how well the plugins did, and where the gaps were — for front-end work AND design ideation.
- U3: Wants industry practice: DESIGN.md, Uber uSpec, Figma + Figma MCP, Claude Design, other tools; then Shopify/Airbnb/Vercel/Atlassian/Netflix/IBM etc.; then Anthropic 5.5 and latest GPT guidance; AGENTS.md; ICAO/SID-STAR/FIS-AFIS phraseology; caveman guidance and evals; TanStack Intent.
- U4: "Let's not cut things please, why be lazy?" — nothing from the evidence may be silently dropped; every finding gets a work item or an explicit, evidence-based disposition.
- U5 (from transcripts, user's own words in the sessions): 2026-10-14 20:25 "Let's lean less on the specs and tests as we build this… two phases of work, exploratory build quick, validate ideas and iterate… Ideation like this shouldn't be so strict about specs and tests. Those come when we narrow it down… avoid regressions." Also 10-08 seo-geo "stop with these tests. It's a waste of time"; 10-14 16:49 "I said I wanted us to iterate first"; "We don't test our CSS per se… We'll worry about visual testing later"; "I need actual examples of what is being approved"; "did you lose that decision. I'm frustrated now"; "Let's stop doing the claude artifacts, we can try locally".

## UB. Uber uSpec — blog + docs fetched [P, LLM-summarized fetch]
- Blog https://www.uber.com/us/en/blog/automate-design-specs/ ; docs https://docs.uspec.design/ ; repo https://github.com/redongreen/uSpec (ownership and license NOT verified).
- Problem: Base design system, 7 stacks (UIKit, SwiftUI, Android XML/Compose, Web React, Go, SDUI); "hundreds of spec pages that all need to stay accurate"; "When those specs fall behind, engineering builds from assumptions".
- Three layers: (1) Agent Skills = domain instruction files with validation rules and reference docs, six specialized skills (Anatomy, API, Properties, Color annotation, Structure, Screen reader; Motion from After Effects); (2) Figma Console MCP, open source, local WebSocket bridge; (3) rendering layer: script populates templates in Figma.
- Pipeline per docs: Extract → Compile → Render. uSpec Extract Figma plugin captures "deterministic evidence" once; `create-component-md` interprets and validates it into a schema-valid JSON contract + concise Markdown ("Component.MD"); `create-*` skills read the generated Markdown, not Figma again ("save thousands of tokens per run").
- Deterministic extraction: token names, variant values, component structure, parent-child, variable modes, layer hierarchy. LLM: a11y semantics classification, token mapping across states, spec organization, platform behavior from provided context.
- Hallucination control: reference libraries loaded first ("the agent doesn't guess at property names — it selects from documented APIs"), structured schemas, real-data grounding, local execution.
- Human-in-the-loop: share link + optional context for non-inferrable states/platform behavior; results render in Figma for review.
- Results: screen-reader spec for 3 platforms "under 2 minutes"; months → days.
- Limits: needs well-structured Figma files, accurate tokens/variables; extract-once means initial capture must be accurate. Roadmap: drift detection, code-to-spec, new spec types.
- Runs in Cursor, Claude Code, Codex.

## UC. TanStack Intent 0.5 — https://tanstack.com/blog/intent-0.5-skills-you-can-maintain [P, summarized fetch]
- Library maintainers ship SKILL.md inside npm packages so skills version 1:1 with code. "It helps to solve the delivery problem. It doesn't, by itself, solve the maintenance problem."
- 0.5 additions: `validate` compiles fenced JS/TS examples in SKILL.md with the TypeScript compiler (missing exports, invalid options, type mismatches); `maintainer review` identifies guidance affected by source changes, tied to specific source+skill versions ("has someone checked this guidance against what changed?" not "is this file old?"); `repair --write` applies mechanical frontmatter fixes only, code changes need review; reusable GitHub checks for validation, generated-file drift, pending source reviews — surface in Actions summary, never auto-apply fixes; agent hooks use local CLI when installed. Skills "belong in the development process".

## IC. ICAO / aviation phraseology analogy [K — from author knowledge, NOT fetched; verify against ICAO Annex 10/11, Doc 4444, Doc 9432 before any normative use]
- Standard words with fixed meanings: affirm, negative, roger (received, not yes), wilco, unable, standby, say again, verify, correction, disregard; avoid "OK".
- Readback/hearback: pilot reads back safety-critical items; controller must verify and correct. A readback nobody checks is theater.
- SID/STAR: published named procedures referenced by name in the clearance; reduce workload, pre-agreed details.
- Lost-communications procedures: predefined behavior when contact is lost. Missed approach/go-around: predefined at decision altitude, not improvised.
- Pilot-in-command authority: may deviate in emergency but must declare and report afterwards.
- Urgency tiers (pan-pan/mayday) with fixed handling.
- IFR (controlled, clearance, controller responsible for separation) vs VFR with FIS/AFIS (information only, no clearances, pilot responsible); IFR can be picked up in the air and cancelled.
- Mapping proposed: sketch = VFR+FIS; promote = pick up IFR clearance; stall/timeouts = lost-comms; retry cap = missed approach; override = declared deviation; closed vocabulary + readback for gate churn. Limits: phraseology exists for noisy voice; rigidity is justified by lives at stake; needs enforcement/training; agents follow prompts so vocabulary must be short.

## CV. "Caveman" prompting — measured
- Skill: https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman (~94k stars per https://enterprisedna.co/resources/ai-pulse/ai-pulse-2026-07-28-a-claude-code-skill-called-caveman-respond-in-terse-fragment/ ). Repo eval [P]: 3 arms (baseline, "Answer concisely", skill), 1 call/arm/prompt on Opus 5.5, tiktoken o200k_base output tokens, fidelity regex checks; claims 65% mean (22–87%) over 10 prompts; self-stated limits: tokenizer approximation, n=1, regex-only fidelity, no cross-model.
- Independent [P, summarized]: https://dev.to/nazecode/i-measured-the-viral-talk-like-a-caveman-token-saver-a-two-word-prompt-got-most-of-it-118a — one C# debugging task, n=3/variant: "Be concise." −28.7%, caveman −42.9%, ultra −63.6%; all correct; skill needs ~10 answers to break even vs two-word prompt.
- JetBrains [P, full page via Playwright]: https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2026/07/speak-to-ai-agents-like-cavemen-tosave-tokens/ (Denis Shiryaev). Harbor 0.17, Claude Code 2.1.200, claude-sonnet-5 effort low, SkillsBench 86/87 tasks, 3 runs, ~240 trials, ~$106. Arm B forced activation (ceiling). Output tokens: smoke 10 tasks k=1 −29.5%; 10 tasks k=3 −6.7%; full 86 (82 clean pairs) k=1 −8.5% (592k→542k). Quality: 64 tied, 10 skill higher, 8 lower, sign test p=0.82; mean score 0.326 vs 0.311. Cost: expected ~−10% but raw totals +11.6% ($40.60 vs $36.39) due to single task crossing 200k long-context tier ($8.29 vs $0.33). Lesson: "Never trust a k=1 eval."
- Others [S]: real coding tasks 14–21% (BetterStack); community reproductions 30–50%; agentic ~8.5%; "Be concise. Return JSON." handles ~60% of savings.
- Brevity paper [S]: arXiv 2604.00025 "Brevity Constraints Reverse Performance Hierarchies in Language Models" — 31 models, 1,485 problems; brevity improves large-model accuracy up to 26 points on some benchmarks; Concise-CoT study [S, unverified] showed GPT-3.5 −27.69% on math.

## RT. rtk (Rust Token Killer) — JetBrains test [P, full page via Playwright]
- https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2026/07/rtk-claude-code-token-savings/ (Part 2, Jul 20 2026). Harbor 0.18, Claude Code 2.1.201, claude-sonnet-5 at low and high effort, rtk v0.43.0 as `rtk init -g` ships (binary + PreToolUse hook + RTK.md), 425 trials, ~$320.
- Claimed −60–90%. Ceiling analysis from replay of 83 transcripts: of 1,056 shell commands, 349 rewritable, 525 no rule (python3, project scripts, loops), 182 skipped on purpose; of 1.9M chars tool output, 20% compressible, 46% shell without rule, 34% Read/Grep bypassing hook; total cap ≈3% of input.
- Measured: low effort, 80 clean pairs: cost +7.6% median (p=0.004), turns +13.8% (p=0.03), cache reads +14.3% (p=0.008), fresh input +3.2% (p=0.23), output +6.7% (ns); heavily-rewritten pairs +24% vs +5%. High effort: cost +0.1% (p=0.99). Quality: 151 paired tasks 10 better/8 worse/133 identical; sign test p=1.0 both efforts. One compatibility failure (glibc) and one broken rewrite class (compound find predicates). `rtk gain` reported 96.2M tokens saved while the bill rose: counterfactual counts raw output (1.2MB cat = 320k "saved"), chars÷4 estimate, cached re-reads at a tenth of price.
- Lessons: "a tool's self-reported savings are a claim about its counterfactual, not about your bill"; paired analysis only; per-task medians + Wilcoxon; exclude errored tasks from both arms; ladder: free transcript replay → wiring check → k=1 smoke → k=3 → full run at each effort. ~80 tasks can only rule out large effects (~700 runs/side for subtle shifts). User's global config (~/.claude/RTK.md) installs rtk with the same hook — an own-workflow paired test is an open item; do not change user config without being asked.

## NF. Netflix + JetBrains IDE intelligence — https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2026/10/how-netflix-made-ai-coding-agents-more-efficient/ (Oct 15 2026) [P, full page; vendor-hosted case study]
- Netflix ADP, GenAI Platform and Agentic SDLC teams plugged JetBrains' headless code-intelligence engine into Claude Code and Codex for Java/Kotlin (esp. JAR boundaries). Netflix built the daemon (keeps index warm, session manager by project root, GraalVM executable) and CLI because the LSP alone isn't callable by an agent.
- Eval: 2 codebases (internal Spring Boot 4/Gradle service; open-source DGS Framework), navigation tasks + end-to-end tasks; models Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol (medium/high effort); metrics tokens + time, LLM-as-judge vs reference change set for end-to-end, deterministic scoring for navigation; outlier tasks excluded from both arms; multiple runs.
- Results: typically 20–30% more efficient, up to ~65% best case (strongest model, high effort, navigation); end-to-end ~21–30%; correctness held or improved; one config's time comparison unrepresentative due to batched search. Numbers are a snapshot.
- Quote: JetBrains' Stukalov: "Agents need a code engine, not a virtual editor" — operations in terms of symbols, diagnostics, test relations, runtime behavior, not cursor positions. Netflix: "there is a benefit to having a deterministic intelligence layer alongside your agent". Netflix plans Python/TS/JS/Go.
- Repo link: commit f10e6b8 "feat(smith): add language-service evidence guidance" already points this direction.
- Not about design/front-end; does not answer Netflix design-system question (only job posting hints at a "design intelligence layer", per S2).

## PL. Repo facts verified in this session
- muse plugin.json, README.md:23, skills/component/SKILL.md:11 all point to "ranger's accessibility hazard taxonomy"; grep for "accessib" finds nothing in plugins/ranger; only shared/references/verification/interface-coverage.md mentions accessibility. [verified by grep]
- 29 of 31 shared/schemas/*.json have a "reasoning" field; all 44 agents mention reasoning/scratchpad; constitution L242 requires `reasoning: string` scratchpad in every schema. [verified by grep]
- ADR index (docs/adr/README.md): 001 four-part structure, 002 EARS output only, 003 cognitive-mode separation ("Do not combine enumeration and judgment in one agent without a new ADR"), 004 immutable schemas (new @n+1), 005 artifact-agnostic gate, 006 byte-identical constitution, 007 persona naming, 008 drop test-first, 009 implementer shape latitude, 010 Wisp Plugins brand. decision-records.md says: write an ADR only when architectural AND expensive-to-reverse/non-obvious; one-line "Do not X without a new ADR" index entry.
- Validation: `just check` = manifests test versions skills-doc reference-size marketplace-check mermaid; Codex files generated via `just marketplace-sync`; harness counterparts per shared/harness-authoring.md.

## MISC. Earlier conversation facts
- Session corpus correction: ~812 jsonl files are mostly subagent transcripts; only ~7 real top-level sessions across the projects; plugin agents used in 2 (orin-dx b8d16e96 09-29..10-03; pages 24655582 10-05..10-16) + vanguard in pages writing-candidates e8f0978b (2026-10-17).
- ~/projects/orin-dx-site holds only brand/ HTML artifacts (no git, no docs); the docs live in ~/projects/pages/docs.

# Draft work packages (WP) — v0, to be extended by unmapped findings

Plugins: courier, mason, muse, navigator, ranger, scribe, sentinel, smith, vanguard, weaver (+ shared/, docs/adr, harnesses/codex).

## G0 Defects and baselines
- WP-01 Fix muse's dangling "ranger accessibility hazard taxonomy" references (plugin.json, README, SKILL.md) — either build the pack (WP-44) or correct the docs.
- WP-02 Migrate muse from verdict@1 to verdict@3 (version bump, Codex counterpart).
- WP-03 Baseline metrics script over transcripts: gate rounds per spec, blocker types (wording vs substantive), time-to-first-visual, post-gate defects, stalls/failed agent tasks, tokens/cost per phase.
- WP-04 Cross-reference link checker in `just check` / mason:audit-plugin (plugin docs referencing things that don't exist).
- WP-05 Correct/verify factual claims in repo docs touched by this evaluation (counts, tier tables).

## G1 Exploration and ideation
- WP-10 ADR(s): exploratory/divergent cognitive mode (amends ADR 003), mode routing, non-binding artifacts.
- WP-11 muse `sketch` skill: option files with stable IDs + status (open/parked/chosen/rejected) + one-line reason; anchor brief re-derived each round; ~3 options default; TBDs allowed; no gate; visibly low-fidelity marker; assumptions list; hard stop before implementation; scratch-dir-only write guard.
- WP-12 Sketch rendering medium and option matrix: local dev server/static pages, Playwright screenshots, side-by-side option boards, brand × theme × viewport matrix from tokens; Artifacts as optional; how sketches land in a repo.
- WP-13 Decision log + cross-session persistence: format, where it lives in consumer repos, surfaced through AGENTS.md routing, retrieval of prior-session decisions, "recorded but not applied" detection, rule candidates pending until human accepts (never promote a single screenshot/comment), conflict with ADR table.
- WP-14 `promote` skill: prototype/sketch → requirement@1 → spec@2; prototype/screenshots kept as visual oracle; change-delta specs; carry decision_ref; resolve TBDs or move to non_goals.
- WP-15 smith `spike` skill: validate that a tool/library/approach works in the stack; throwaway marker; skip plan/spec/mutator/reviewer/exit-gate; report verified vs unverified; smoke-check evidence recipe; promote or discard.
- WP-16 Direction-commit and anti-slop controls: propose ~4 distinct directions → user picks; named aesthetic; ban lists; rejection clauses; second-order slop patterns; taste dials (variance/motion/density); deterministic slop scanner.
- WP-17 Visual critique / design-review agent: Playwright multi-viewport critic, severity tiers (P0–P3), user-impact language with screenshots, hierarchy/contrast checks; distinct from spec audit.
- WP-18 Mode router: shape / sketch / spike / implement / review / copy / harden / promote; exploration modes read-only or sketch-only; explicit authority labeling ("cleared by"); IFR/VFR framing; ability to enter/leave gated mode explicitly.
- WP-19 Exploration → hardening handoff: characterization tests, pin behavior, hardening checklist (empty/loading/error states, a11y, copy truth, responsive), "harden" mode keeps direction and fixes state/a11y.
- WP-20 Copy/voice workflow: copy review agent/skill, case-study truth audit, voice consistency, content provenance (see WP-43).
- WP-21 Research for design (vanguard): visual/competitive sourcing, prior-art boards, keep the recon→reader→synthesizer path that worked; framing questions sharply.

## G2 Spec and visual intent
- WP-30 ADR + `spec@2`: token references `{path}`, visual references (Figma node, Storybook story id, screenshot path), per-state render references, decision_ref, supersedes links; keep falsifiable criteria; no TBD in spec (TBD only in sketch).
- WP-31 Design-intent artifact: small routed files (DESIGN.md-compatible front matter tokens + prose + Do/Don't + rejection clauses), lint/export via optional CLI, `coverage-gaps` file, exemplar good/bad PRs; component facts via lookup not monolith.
- WP-32 Ground-truth extraction step (recon): tokens, props, measured geometry from repo/running page/prototype → facts file consumed by drafter/planner/verifier; compile examples (validate); version-tied reviews.
- WP-33 Reference tables loaded before drafting: ARIA APG patterns, keyboard maps, platform a11y APIs; "never write from memory" hard rule.
- WP-34 Human-reviewable spec rendering and approval evidence: dual format (JSON + readable), rendered approval boards, "show, don't describe" before approval.
- WP-35 Optional design-source adapter: design-source@1 (figma|screenshot|html|description|none); capability-detected Figma MCP adapter (metadata first, then node), Storybook MCP, Code Connect-equivalent checks (token use, component reuse), rules-file generator.
- WP-36 Spec/plan size and stall guards: size caps, chunked writes, split specs, supersession handling and stale-spec cleanup.

## G3 Verification evidence

The catalog is done, and two verification passes are still running. It covers 144 work packages: 60 from the draft and 84 proposed across the five maps. None were renumbered or deleted.

- **8 are merged** into another work package, each with a reason. About 20 more overlap another one and are kept, with the reason stated.
- **The waves add up to 144:**

| Wave | Theme | WPs |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Defects, baselines, measurement | 21 |
| 1 | Exploration modes | 19 |
| 2 | Gate hygiene and orchestration | 27 |
| 3 | Visual intent and evidence | 43 |
| 4 | Prompt, model, Codex, AGENTS.md, distribution | 27 |
| 5 | Consumer-repo and research follow-ups | 7 |

- **10 new ADRs are needed**, drafted as proposals:
  - N1: exploratory mode, which amends ADR 003.
  - N2: `spec@2` and design intent.
  - N3: `workspace-manifest@2` and render evidence.
  - N4: gate hygiene and overrides.
  - N5: orchestrator authority and trust.
  - N6: the `reasoning` field.
  - N7: decision log and rule promotion.
  - N8: Codex role cards and AGENTS.md.
  - N9: skill distribution.
  - N10: prompt-structure ablation, conditional on its result.
- **Wave 1 needs only N1.** Wave 2 needs N4 and N5. Wave 3 needs N2 and N3, and its schema bumps ship as one bundle. That keeps the exploration modes unblocked by the larger schema work.

The catalog resolves 20 conflicts, and these are its recommendations. They are defaults I can change:
- **Options:** 3 per round, and 4 directions only at the first direction-commit.
- **Parallel writers:** default 3, up to 5 for disjoint work, and larger batches only for independent migration runs.
- **Reviewer scope:** scanners report everything, a separate cheap stage filters, and gates stay scoped to stated requirements. The measurement work (WP-60) should test this before the gate-hygiene change lands.
- **Codex role cards:** the draft said "TOML subagents," but `shared/harness-authoring.md` forbids TOML as a plugin contract, so the plan uses markdown role cards.
- **Opus gate effort:** don't act on the vendor claim that gates can drop to medium until WP-63 measures it.

One placement I disagree with: the catalog put `promote` (WP-14) and the visual critic (WP-17) in Wave 3 because they depend on `spec@2` and render evidence. Your priority is exploration, and a sketch mode with no way to carry a chosen design forward is half a loop. I'd add a lightweight promote to Wave 1 that produces a requirement and a brief, and keep the full `spec@2` version in Wave 3. The catalog already uses a lightweight screenshot check inside the sketch skill for the same reason. I'll build that into the final plan unless you object.

I'm waiting on the two verification passes (transcript and repo claims, and web and documentation claims) before assembling the deliverable.

  - v0 Design Systems 2.0 launched 2026-06-25, not Feb 5.
  - The Figma Starter limit is now 20 calls per month, not 6.
  - `run-story-tests` is not a current Storybook tool name; use `test-run`.

  - "Skills too prescriptive" appears only on the Fable 5 page, not on other tiers' pages.
  - Anthropic's verification advice is per-model, not one rule. Opus 5 says remove explicit verification; Sonnet 5.5 at low effort needs a real-check paragraph; Fable 5 recommends fresh-context verifier subagents.
  - The Sonnet 5.5 one-third cost saving was measured at `max` effort.
  - Codex: GPT-6.1 Sol is the recommended model, and GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna remain selectable, so the two sources are not contradictory. The AGENTS.md cap is confirmed at 32 KiB by default and is configurable.

  - Claude Design: handoff to Claude Code, exports and design-system import are confirmed; the quota burn and drift at revision 4-5 are not on the product page.

  - Atlassian's table (7.21M for DESIGN.md vs 3.75M MCP, 4.43M skill, 4.20M none) and the CLI vs MCP 8%/8%.
  - Vercel's 39 vs 91 failures (57% fewer), from only 6 pages.
  - Google DESIGN.md: alpha, `@google/design.md`, 11 lint rules, 8 sections, dtcg export, Apache-2.0.
  - uSpec: `redongreen/uSpec`, MIT, listed as open source on GitHub in Uber's blog.
  - `get_variable_defs` is available on both Figma servers.
  - DTCG 2025.10 is stable.
  - Deque's 57% is by issue volume, from a 2021 study.

  - Spawn-depth env var `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` defaults to 3. `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENTS_PER_SESSION` was removed in v2.1.224.
  - Model defaults: Fable 5.1 high, Opus 5.5 medium (thinking always on), Sonnet 5.5 high on the API, Haiku 5.5 medium.
  
  **Unverifiable**
  - Shopify Dispatch and Airbnb numbers.
  - The Figma 25k response cap.
  - GPT-6 `none` effort.
  - Atlassian's earlier 34%/16% figures.
  - I read the DESIGN.md lint rules from the README only and did not run the linter.

# Work-package catalog (consolidated)

Inputs: WP-draft.md (60 WPs) plus proposed WPs from MAP-1 (12), MAP-2 (15), MAP-3 (18), MAP-4 (21), MAP-5 (18). Total 144 WPs, none renumbered, none deleted. 8 are marked merged-into (their scope is kept in the surviving WP; the id stays valid for the matrices).

Conventions used in the table
- Evidence = number of matrix table rows (lines starting with `|`) in MAP-1..5 that contain the id. WP-112, WP-510, WP-517, WP-518 show 0 because they were only introduced in the proposal sections.
- ADR column: `amends N` means an accepted ADR's guardrail is touched (the record is not rewritten; per docs/adr/README.md it is marked or superseded by a new one). `new N1..N10` are the proposed new ADRs listed in section 3.2. `none` means a constitution/docs change that needs no ADR.
- Schema column: a new schema or schema version is needed (ADR 004: published schemas are immutable, add `@n+1`). Bundle all bumps in one release (spec@2, plan@2, verdict@4, workspace-manifest@2, requirement@2) to limit consumer churn.
- Codex column: Y if a skill, agent, schema, or route changes (harness-authoring.md: read the counterpart, record the change record, run `just marketplace-sync`). N for docs, tooling, eval, research, and consumer-repo work. Codex role cards are markdown resources, not TOML (see conflict K9).
- Size: S under 1 day, M 1 to 3 days, L over 3 days or multi-plugin.
- W = proposed wave (0 to 5), see section 3.

## 3. Sequencing

### 3.1 Waves

Wave counts (computed from the W column, merged ids included): W0 = 21, W1 = 19, W2 = 27, W3 = 43, W4 = 27, W5 = 7; total 144. Merged ids (91, 112, 202, 208, 214, 215, 308, 518) sit in the wave of the WP they merged into, except 91 and 518 which sit in W0.

**Wave 0: defects, baselines, measurement.** Reason: everything else needs a baseline to prove improvement and the cheap defects are independent of design choices.
- Defects: WP-01, WP-02, WP-05, WP-510 (policy text only), WP-56 (find why agents were unused before adding more), WP-61 (+518).
- Measurement: WP-03 (+91), WP-60, WP-514, WP-515, WP-516, WP-517, WP-422, WP-109.
- Tooling guards: WP-04, WP-440, WP-508.
- Research hygiene: WP-90, WP-401.
- ADRs preceding: none required; N6 draft can start in parallel with WP-61.

**Wave 1: exploration modes (user's stated priority).** Reason: D-04/D-11 show the pipeline was abandoned for lack of sketch/spike modes and cost, so this wave carries the most value. Gate-free, scratch-only, so it depends only on the exploration ADR and not on schema bumps.
- ADR N1 (WP-10) first, then WP-18 (router) and WP-11 (sketch), then WP-12, WP-15, WP-16, WP-19, WP-104, WP-13 (decision log, needs N7 draft), WP-21, WP-211, WP-305, WP-306, WP-309 (+208), WP-314, WP-315, WP-427, WP-512 (+308 write guard portion).
- Parallel: WP-11 and WP-15 are different plugins (muse, smith) and can run concurrently once N1 is accepted.
- Codex counterparts are done per WP (WP-70 checklist), not deferred.

**Wave 2: gate hygiene and orchestration.** Reason: independent of exploration; benefits both the old and new flows. Needs measurements from Wave 0 to avoid unmeasured policy (K2).
- ADRs N4 (gate hygiene, override) and N5 (orchestrator authority) first.
- WP-50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55 (+214), 57, 58, 36, 106, 107, 108 (+202), 201, 203, 205, 209, 210, 212, 310, 317, 407, 413, 425, 506.
- WP-212 and WP-51 may need verdict@4: fold into the Wave 3 schema bundle if possible.

**Wave 3: visual intent and evidence.** Reason: biggest schema work, builds on the Wave 1 learning (what promotes cleanly) and Wave 2 gate rules.
- ADRs N2 (spec@2 and design intent) and N3 (manifest@2 and render evidence) first.
- Schemas: WP-30, 31, 40, 41, 103, 35 as one bundle (spec@2, plan@2, manifest@2, render-evidence@1, design-intent@1, design-source@1).
- Then: WP-14 (promote), 32, 33, 34, 42 (+112), 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 17, 20 (+215), 101, 102, 105, 110, 111, 204, 206, 207, 213, 301-304, 307, 312, 316, 318, 404, 412, 418, 437, 73, 67.

**Wave 4: prompt, model, Codex, AGENTS.md, distribution.** Reason: ablation and prompt edits would invalidate Wave 1 to 3 evals if run first; they need the eval harness plus stable agents.
- ADR N10 (conditional on WP-62 results), N8 (Codex role cards and AGENTS.md), N9 (distribution).
- WP-62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 70 (final sweep), 71, 72, 74, 311, 402, 403, 405, 406, 408, 409, 411, 421, 501-505, 507, 509, 511, 513.

**Wave 5: consumer-repo and research follow-ups.** Reason: not plugin changes, or lowest value until the tooling exists.
- WP-80, 81, 82, 68, 313, 414, 444.

### 3.2 ADR schedule (10 new, 3 conditional)

| ADR | Covers | Amends or relates | Must precede |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| N1 Exploratory mode | WP-10, 11, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 304, 444 | amends 003 (guardrail: no enumeration+judgment mix; new mode is divergent, non-binding) | Wave 1 |
| N2 spec@2 and design intent | WP-30, 31, 35, 301, 302 | ADR 004 (new version, no in-place edit); 005 unaffected | Wave 3 schemas |
| N3 manifest@2 and render evidence | WP-40, 41, 32, 207, 312 | keeps 005 (artifact-agnostic gate) | Wave 3 |
| N4 Gate hygiene and overrides | WP-50, 51, 212, 310, 413 | clarifies constitution Epistemic Stopping and Sentinel Retry sections | Wave 2 |
| N5 Orchestrator authority and trust | WP-55, 214, 308/512, 317, 407, 425, 509 | extends Trust Boundaries; no existing ADR changed | Wave 2 |
| N6 `reasoning` field policy | WP-61, 518, 505 | ADR 004 (@n+1 for ~29 schemas) | any schema bump after Wave 0 result |
| N7 Decision log and rule promotion | WP-13, 201, 412, 414 | relation to docs/adr table; must state log is not an ADR | Wave 1 for WP-13 |
| N8 Codex role-card and AGENTS.md | WP-70, 71, 510 | aligns with shared/harness-authoring.md | Wave 4 |
| N9 Skill distribution | WP-72, 408 | none | Wave 4 |
| N10 Prompt-structure ablation outcome (conditional) | WP-62, 64, 507 | amends 001, 006 only if ablation justifies | Wave 4 edits |

Rule: any WP whose guardrail row in docs/adr/README.md would be broken (003 combine modes; 004 edit schema in place; 001 add `<role>`; 002 EARS outside output; 007 rename a skill) must have its ADR accepted before implementation starts.

### 3.3 Wave sizes (computed from the W column)

W0 21, W1 19, W2 27, W3 43, W4 27, W5 7 (total 144). Note WP-14 (promote) and WP-17 (visual critic) are tagged W3 in the table although grouped with exploration, because they depend on spec@2 and render-evidence; Wave 1 uses a lightweight screenshot self-check inside WP-11 instead.

| K2 | Reviewers restricted to correctness (over-report risk) vs WP-50 scanners report all then filter | MAP-3 R4-06 | Keep "report all with confidence/severity" for scanners (cheap, high recall); add a separate cheap filter stage; restrict gate/reviewer prompts to stated requirements. Test both in WP-60 before landing WP-50. | R4-06; contradiction 6 in MAP-3 |

The 3-5 is practitioner advice for merge safety, the 5-30 is capability; validate in WP-55 pilot. | MAP-3 contradiction 5; B-11/B-93 (26 forks) |
| K4 | Opus gates `high` in constitution vs Opus 5.5 medium >= Opus 5 high; Fable never gates vs Fable 5.1 low competitive | MAP-5 C-4 | Do not change tiers on vendor claims; run WP-63 effort sweep after WP-60; WP-501 adds version stamps. Until then keep constitution. | M1-19/20/79/103 |
| K5 | Over-verification on Opus producers (WP-64) vs under-verification on sonnet/haiku (WP-506) | MAP-5 C-1 | Make verification rules model-conditioned; ship WP-506 first for sonnet/medium agents (the majority); do WP-64's removal only on Opus. | M1-28, M1-29 |
